title: Beyond thought
hookLine: by thinking, God can't be reached, even by thinking a hundred thousand times (Japji 1)
tomorrow: what hour, what season was the world made? who knows?

cards: The shower: water running, door shut, and for a minute the thinking stops. The old Sikh stories of Guru Nanak's life, the janamsakhis, start his teaching at water too.
In Sultanpur, they say, he went into the river Bein at dawn to bathe, and didn't come out. People searched the banks. Three days, nothing.
When he came back, the stories give his first words as: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.

teach.h: OUT OF THE RIVER, A SONG.
teach.b: Where had he been? In God's presence, the stories say, and what came out of it was song.
The Japji, the hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib and the Sikh morning prayers, has a first stanza that sounds like a man who has stopped trying to think his way there.

By thinking, it says, He can't be thought, though you think a hundred thousand times. Some Sikh scholars read that first word as cleansing instead: bathe a hundred thousand times, and you still aren't made pure.
Either way, by keeping silent, the inner silence doesn't come, though you sit lost in focus. The hunger of the hungry isn't eased, though you pile up whole worlds.
A hundred thousand clevernesses, and not one goes with you. So how do you become true? How does the wall of falsehood come down?
The stanza's last line answers: by walking in the hukam, the order, the will, which is written with you.
In Sikh teaching, then, God isn't reached by more thinking, more silence or more getting; the way is to live inside the hukam, the divine order, with your whole life.
Notice the shape: the Japji asks a huge question, how to become true, and answers it in a single line.
Thought isn't the enemy. It just isn't the road.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji of Guru Nanak as the first of the morning prayers, the Nitnem; it also opens the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: what thinking, even endlessly, can't reach
an idea too clever to put into words
a calm state after hours of meditation

games.q: the Japji's first stanza: tap the pairs.
p: can't think Him, a hundred thousand times

s: the Japji says enough thinking will lead you to God
by thinking, He can't be thought, though one think a hundred thousand times.
the janamsakhis say Nanak vanished into a river before he began to teach
the stories say he went into the Bein and came back after three days.
the Japji says sitting in silence is the way
even silence, it says, doesn't bring the inner silence; the way is the hukam.

games.q: a friend meditates for hours to quiet her mind, and says it isn't working. what does the Japji's first stanza add?
o: silence alone isn't the road; the Japji points to walking in the hukam.
sit longer; the Japji promises silence comes after enough hours.
give up quiet altogether; the Japji calls it worthless.
games.why: the stanza says silence doesn't bring the inner silence, though one sit absorbed; it ends on walking in the hukam.

practice: Run a tap, or pour a glass of water slowly, and just listen. When a thought arrives, don't argue with it and don't follow it; go back to the sound of the water. Let the sound do what the thinking can't.

orig.s: ਸੋਚੈ ਸੋਚਿ ਨ ਹੋਵਈ ਜੇ ਸੋਚੀ ਲਖ ਵਾਰ

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji stanza 1: by thinking, He can't be thought, though one think a hundred thousand times.

carryVoice: Keep this: beyond thought, and inside the hukam, where the walking happens. The Japji, one of five.

sources.ref: Japji, stanza (pauri) 1, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1 (by thinking He cannot be thought, though one think a hundred thousand times; by silence, inner silence is not won; the hunger of the hungry is not appeased; of a hundred thousand clevernesses not one goes along; how to become true, how the wall of falsehood is broken: by walking in the hukam, written with us)
Puratan Janamsakhi (and other janamsakhis): Guru Nanak at the river Bein in Sultanpur, three days' absence, 'there is no Hindu, there is no Musalman'
